_about: Arm B disposition scenarios. One patient per scenario. The standard program protocol in data/protocol.json applies unless the visit text states otherwise.
Every lab value is a generator spec drawn from data/bands.json, exactly as in Arm A; 'focus' names the master-table row the answer key leans on and supplies the reference range and source.
Placeholders {key} are filled everywhere: patient card, visit, labs, rationale, follow-up.
tier: 1 emergent ED transport now | 2 same-day evaluation, non-emergent | 3 PCP or clinic within 24-48 hours | 4 manage in place with follow-up or care coordination.
followUp: one four-option question after the tier. Same construction rules as Arm A multiple-choice items.
Ketones are urine dipstick results only in Arm B. A lab value is one input among several, never the deciding factor on its own.

tiers.4: Manage in place with follow-up or care coordination

scenarios.title: Stable chronic hyponatremia

patient.living: Lives alone in a single-story house; a neighbor checks in most days.
baselines: Sodium {nab} on every panel for the past two years
Weight 61 kg at last visit (dry weight 60–62 kg)

social.transport: Daughter drives her to appointments; lives 40 minutes away
social.adherence: Pill organizer filled by daughter; rarely misses

patient.goals: Full treatment; strongly prefers to avoid hospital

visit.reason: Scheduled monthly heart failure visit.
visit.history: Feels her usual self. No new breathlessness, no orthopnea beyond her usual two pillows, no swelling change.
visit.vitals: HR 72 regular, BP 132/78, RR 16, SpO2 95% on air, temp 36.8 °C, weight 61 kg
visit.exam: Alert and oriented. Lungs clear. Trace ankle edema, unchanged. No focal deficit.

scenarios.rationale: The number is band 2 on the table, and a medic sees a sodium in the 120s and reaches for transport. But she is at her documented baseline, asymptomatic, at dry weight, with nothing new on exam. Rate of change outranks the absolute number. Document, trend, keep the next scheduled visit. Correcting chronic hyponatremia quickly risks osmotic demyelination, so a fluid bolus would be the wrong intervention even in hospital.
factors: Sodium unchanged from a two-year baseline
No neurological symptoms
Weight at dry weight, exam unchanged
Reliable daily contact at home

followUp.stem: Which finding on a future visit would move this patient's sodium from a trend-it number to a same-day problem?

options.text: A reading of 125 mEq/L at a routine recheck
A new SSRI prescribed with the same reading
A drop of 8 mEq/L in days with new confusion
A 1 kg weight gain over the past month

followUp.rationale: An acute fall with symptoms is what changes the disposition; the absolute number and a single-kilogram weight drift do not. A new SSRI is a reason to recheck, not by itself a same-day trigger.

scenarios.title: Dialysis patient between sessions

patient.living: Lives with his wife in a ground-floor apartment.
diagnoses: End-stage renal disease on hemodialysis (Monday, Wednesday, Friday)
baselines: Pre-dialysis potassium runs 5.3–5.6 mEq/L on the dialysis unit's records
Last ECG on file: no peaked T waves, QRS 96 ms

social.transport: Dialysis transport service; wife drives otherwise
social.adherence: Good; misses sevelamer when eating out

visit.reason: Routine visit on a Tuesday (non-dialysis day).
visit.history: Feels well. Ate a normal dinner last night. No palpitations, weakness or cramps.
visit.vitals: HR 78 regular, BP 146/84, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.6 °C
visit.exam: Fistula thrill present. Lungs clear. No edema. 12-lead ECG: unchanged from the tracing on file.

scenarios.rationale: A dialysis patient at 5.4 on a non-dialysis day is expected, matches his unit's records, and his ECG is unchanged. Medics trained on acute hyperkalemia read this as a crisis; it is his baseline. Document the value and the ECG, confirm tomorrow's dialysis, and move on. The dangerous version of this number is the CKD patient recently started on spironolactone or an ARB, where it climbs over days.
factors: Value inside his documented pre-dialysis range
ECG unchanged from baseline tracing
Dialysis scheduled tomorrow
No symptoms

followUp.stem: He mentions he has been drinking a 'potassium-rich' vegetable juice his son recommended. What should the paramedic do?

options.text: Advise stopping it and notify the dialysis unit
Arrange same-day evaluation for the extra potassium
No action; tomorrow's dialysis will clear it
Recheck the potassium two hours after a glass

followUp.rationale: Dietary potassium in a dialysis patient is a real risk and an education item, but today's value and ECG are fine. Stop the juice, tell the unit so the dietitian follows up, and keep the disposition where it is.

scenarios.title: Long-standing type 2 diabetes running high

patient.living: Lives with his adult son; son works days.
baselines: Glucometer log: 230–280 mg/dL at most readings for the past month

social.adherence: Admits skipping glipizide 'when I feel fine'

visit.reason: Referred by his clinic after a high fingerstick reported by phone.
visit.history: Feels normal. Eating and drinking normally, passing urine normally. No vomiting, no abdominal pain, no fever.
visit.vitals: HR 80, BP 138/82, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.7 °C
visit.exam: Alert, well hydrated, mucous membranes moist. Abdomen soft. Breathing unlabored.

scenarios.rationale: Poor control, not an emergency. A long-standing type 2 diabetic running 230–280 all day with negative ketones, eating and drinking, and no new illness is a medication-adherence conversation and a provider phone consult about the regimen. Medics routinely over-transport this patient. Ketones are what separate this picture from evolving ketoacidosis; they are negative.
factors: Value matches a month of log readings
Urine ketones negative
Eating, drinking, well hydrated, no illness
Adherence gap identified as the cause

followUp.stem: Which teaching point is the priority on this visit?

options.text: Taking glipizide daily even when he feels well
Checking urine ketones every morning before food
Cutting carbohydrates until readings are under 140
Holding metformin whenever a reading passes 250

followUp.rationale: The cause of the pattern is skipped doses. Ketone checks belong to sick days, not routine mornings; diet advice comes from the clinic; and metformin is held for acute illness threatening perfusion, not for a high reading.

scenarios.title: Fall, and a dipstick nobody needed

patient.living: Lives alone in a bungalow with a loose hallway rug.
baselines: No prior urine testing on file

social.transport: No car; relies on a friend
social.cognition: Intact; scored normally at the last clinic screen

patient.goals: Full treatment; wants to stay independent

visit.reason: Referred after a fall yesterday; tripped on the rug, landed on her hip, got up unaided.
visit.history: No head strike, no loss of consciousness. Mild hip bruising. No dysuria, frequency, urgency or suprapubic pain. No fever. A neighbor 'made her' do a dipstick this morning.
visit.vitals: HR 74, BP 140/80, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.9 °C
visit.exam: Bruise over the left greater trochanter, full painless range of motion, walks without a limp. Orthostatic vitals normal. Neurological exam normal.

labs.label: Urine dipstick
labs.text: nitrites positive, leukocyte esterase positive, no blood, no protein

scenarios.rationale: The fall is mechanical, with no injury needing imaging and normal orthostatics; the fix is the rug and a falls-prevention referral. The dipstick is asymptomatic bacteriuria: positive with no urinary symptoms in a non-pregnant older adult, and it does not warrant antibiotics. Treating it drives resistance, C. difficile and avoidable transport. Nearly everyone gets this wrong, so the correct answer is to do nothing about the urine and keep looking at the fall.
factors: Mechanical fall, no head strike, normal exam and orthostatics
No urinary symptoms and no fever
Positive dipstick equals colonization in this setting
Home hazard identified

followUp.stem: What should be done about the dipstick result?

options.text: Send a culture and treat only if it grows
Provider consult for a three-day antibiotic
Document the result and do not treat it
Repeat the dipstick at next week's visit

followUp.rationale: No symptoms, no treatment, and no culture either: a positive culture in this setting would only invite unnecessary antibiotics. Confusion alone, if it appeared later, would still not make it symptomatic.

scenarios.title: Warfarin and the new salad habit
scenarios.focus: Warfarin — dietary and drug influences on the INR

baselines: INR {inrb} at each of the last four checks on an unchanged dose
No missed doses recorded in her anticoagulation log

visit.reason: Scheduled INR check.
visit.history: No bleeding, bruising, falls, new medications or antibiotics. Proudly reports she has 'finally started eating healthy' with a large salad every day for three weeks.
visit.vitals: HR 68 irregular, BP 128/76, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air
visit.exam: No bruising or petechiae. No calf tenderness or swelling. Neurologically normal.

scenarios.rationale: Subtherapeutic, not bleeding. The direction is the teaching point: more dietary vitamin K means more antagonism of the warfarin and a lower INR, so a new daily salad has pulled her below target and she is at thrombotic risk, not bleeding risk. Band 1: a dose review per the anticoagulation protocol on a provider phone order, a recheck in about a week, and teach-back. Nothing here needs a clinic chair.
factors: INR below target with a clear dietary explanation
No bleeding, no thrombotic symptoms
Reliable patient with an accurate log
Dose adjustment available by phone order

followUp.stem: What is the right counseling message about the salads?

options.text: Keep the intake steady from week to week
Stop the salads until the INR is back in range
Eat them only on days the warfarin is skipped
Switch to fruit, which has no effect on the INR

followUp.rationale: Consistency rather than avoidance: a stable diet can be dosed around and a fluctuating one cannot. Skipping warfarin to accommodate greens, or bouncing the diet around, is how INRs become unpredictable.

scenarios.title: The compensated retainer

patient.living: Lives with his wife; home oxygen 2 L/min by nasal cannula.
baselines: Venous gas six months ago: pH {phb}, pCO2 {pco2b}, bicarbonate {hco3b}
Two pillows at night, walks to the mailbox with rests

social.adherence: Good with inhalers; uses oxygen as prescribed

patient.goals: Full treatment; has discussed that he does not want long-term ventilation

visit.reason: Scheduled respiratory visit.
visit.history: At his usual breathlessness. Sputum unchanged in color and amount. Sleeping on two pillows as always. No headache, no drowsiness.
visit.vitals: HR 84, BP 136/80, RR 20, SpO2 90% on 2 L/min, temp 36.7 °C
visit.exam: Alert, conversational in full sentences. Prolonged expiration, scattered wheeze, unchanged. No asterixis. Mild ankle edema, unchanged.

scenarios.rationale: The flagship case. The pCO2 is band 2 and a medic wants to assist ventilation, but the bicarbonate has risen to match and the pH sits inside range: fully compensated chronic respiratory acidosis, identical to his gas six months ago. He is at his usual breathlessness, alert, on his usual oxygen, with unchanged sputum. This is his normal. Document it as baseline so the next crew does not transport him for it.
factors: pH in range with a raised bicarbonate: compensated, therefore chronic
Gas matches the baseline on file
Mentation, sputum, saturation and exam all at baseline
Home oxygen and inhalers used as prescribed

followUp.stem: Which change on a later visit would make this gas an acute-on-chronic emergency?

options.text: pCO2 up to 62 with the same pH and bicarbonate
pH down to 7.24 with new daytime drowsiness
Bicarbonate up to 35 with an unchanged pH
SpO2 of 88% on his usual 2 L/min oxygen

followUp.rationale: Uncompensated means new: a falling pH with rising pCO2 and falling mentation is acute-on-chronic respiratory failure. A slightly higher pCO2 with a stable pH, a higher bicarbonate, or a saturation inside his usual range are all consistent with his chronic state.

scenarios.title: Too-good control in an 88-year-old

patient.living: Lives alone in senior housing; meals delivered at noon.
baselines: Two fingerstick readings under 70 mg/dL recorded by the housing nurse in the past month

social.support: Housing nurse visits weekly; niece by phone
social.adherence: Takes pills from a blister pack; sometimes skips lunch
social.cognition: Mild impairment; manages her own medications with the blister pack

patient.goals: Wants to stay in her apartment; has said she fears another fall more than anything

visit.reason: Referred by the housing nurse because of the low readings.
visit.history: Reports feeling 'shaky and sweaty' before lunch twice last week, better after eating. No falls this month.
visit.vitals: HR 70, BP 134/76, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.6 °C
visit.exam: Alert, oriented to person and place. Gait steady with walker. No focal deficit.

scenarios.rationale: An HbA1c near 6 in an 88-year-old on a sulfonylurea who skips lunch is not good control; it is a hypoglycemia risk in a patient for whom a deliberately looser target is appropriate, and she is already symptomatic twice a week. Paramedics read the low number as success. Nothing is a same-day emergency today: the fingerstick is fine and she is well. The action is a provider phone consult to relax the target and reduce or stop the glipizide, plus a plan for the skipped lunches.
factors: HbA1c below any sensible target for her age and frailty
Documented hypoglycemic episodes on a sulfonylurea
Skipped meals and cognitive impairment raise the risk
Fall history makes hypoglycemia dangerous

followUp.stem: Which medication change should the paramedic propose to the provider?

options.text: Reduce or stop the glipizide dose
Stop the metformin, keep the glipizide
Add a bedtime long-acting insulin
Move the losartan to the evening dose

followUp.rationale: The sulfonylurea is the hypoglycemia driver. Metformin does not cause hypoglycemia on its own; insulin would add risk; the losartan is irrelevant.

scenarios.title: Missed lactulose

medications: Lactulose 30 mL three times daily, titrated to 2–3 soft stools
Acetaminophen 500 mg as needed, maximum 2 g daily
baselines: Ammonia {nh3b} at discharge two months ago, when oriented and walking
Usual mental status: fully oriented, manages his own medications

social.support: Brother works nights, home during the day
social.adherence: Dislikes the lactulose; has stopped it before

visit.reason: Brother called: 'he seems a bit slow.'
visit.history: Stopped lactulose three days ago because of cramping. No bowel movement in four days. No vomiting, no black stools, no fever, no abdominal pain.
visit.vitals: HR 76, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.8 °C
visit.exam: Oriented to person, place and date; slightly slow to answer. No asterixis. Walks unaided. Abdomen soft, mildly distended, no tenderness. No melena on history.

labs.label: Ammonia (send-out from this morning's clinic draw, reported by phone)

scenarios.rationale: Grade 1 encephalopathy from a missed lactulose and constipation, which is the commonest precipitant and the easiest one a paramedic can fix in the home. He is oriented, walking, not vomiting and not bleeding. Restart the lactulose today, titrate to two or three soft stools, consult the provider by phone, and revisit tomorrow. The ammonia correlates poorly with the grade of encephalopathy; the patient is treated, not the number. Somnolence, an inability to take the lactulose, or any bleeding would make this emergent.
factors: Oriented and walking; mild slowing only
Clear precipitant: stopped lactulose, no stool in four days
No GI bleeding, infection or dehydration
Brother available to supervise the restart

followUp.stem: Reviewing his list, which discharge instruction found in the record should be raised with the provider?

options.text: A note limiting dietary protein to 40 g a day
The acetaminophen ceiling set at 2 g a day
Lactulose titrated to stools, not a fixed dose
Propranolol continued after variceal banding

followUp.rationale: Protein restriction in hepatic encephalopathy is obsolete and considered harmful. The 2 g acetaminophen ceiling is correct in liver disease, lactulose is properly titrated to stools, and propranolol is standard after banding.

scenarios.title: A culture nobody owns
scenarios.focus: Pending cultures and outstanding results at discharge

diagnoses: Community-acquired pneumonia, discharged two days ago after a four-day admission
baselines: Discharge summary: blood cultures drawn on admission listed as 'pending'; no clinician named as responsible for follow-up

visit.reason: Post-discharge visit within 48 hours.
visit.history: Improving: cough less, eating, no fever since discharge. Finishing the antibiotic.
visit.vitals: HR 82, BP 130/78, RR 18, SpO2 93% on air (baseline 92–94%), temp 36.9 °C
visit.exam: Crackles at the right base, improving per his account. No respiratory distress.

scenarios.rationale: Clinically he is recovering and stays home. The finding on this visit is not a lab value at all: an admission blood culture that will finalize after discharge with no named person watching for it. That is a transitions-of-care failure the paramedic is positioned to catch. The action is a coordination one, contacting the discharging service or the primary provider to establish who owns the result. A student who reaches for a clinical disposition here has missed the point. The steroid-driven glucose is expected on prednisone.
factors: Clinically improving on treatment
Outstanding result with no documented owner
Glucose elevation explained by the prednisone taper
Wife can relay a result if called

followUp.stem: Who should the paramedic contact first about the pending culture?

options.text: The hospital laboratory, to release the result
The discharging service or the primary provider
The pharmacy, to extend the antibiotic course
The infection control nurse at the hospital

followUp.rationale: A result outstanding with no documented owner is fixed by naming an owner: the discharging team or the PCP. The laboratory does not interpret results, the pharmacy cannot act without an order, and infection control is not the treating clinician.

scenarios.title: Stable eGFR, unreviewed medication list

baselines: eGFR {egfr} on the last three annual panels, unchanged
Creatinine {crb} on the most recent panel

social.support: Son daily by phone, visits twice a week

visit.reason: Enrollment visit for the program; medication reconciliation.
visit.history: Feels well. Some daytime drowsiness he attributes to age. No falls.
visit.vitals: HR 70, BP 128/74, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air
visit.exam: Alert. Mild bilateral foot numbness, chronic. No edema.

scenarios.rationale: The eGFR is stable stage 3a and not a disposition question; it is the number that governs drug dosing, and this list has three drugs that accumulate as clearance falls: gabapentin, a sulfonylurea and allopurinol. His daytime drowsiness may be the gabapentin. This is a reconciliation catch handled by a provider phone consult, not a visit to anyone.
factors: eGFR stable for three years
Three renally cleared drugs on the list
Drowsiness as a possible dosing symptom
No acute findings

followUp.stem: Which drug on his list is least affected by his kidney function?

options.text: Gabapentin
Glipizide
Allopurinol
Amlodipine

followUp.rationale: Amlodipine is cleared by the liver. Gabapentin, sulfonylureas and allopurinol all accumulate as clearance falls and need dose review at this eGFR.

scenarios.title: Expected creatinine rise on lisinopril

medications: Lisinopril 10 mg daily, started two weeks ago
baselines: Creatinine {crb} the day the lisinopril was started

visit.reason: Two-week lab recheck requested by the prescribing provider.
visit.history: Feels well. Passing urine normally. No dizziness.
visit.vitals: HR 72, BP 126/78, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air
visit.exam: Well hydrated. No edema.

scenarios.rationale: A rise of up to about 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor is expected and is not a reason to stop the drug; this rise is under 25%, band 1, with a normal potassium and a well patient. The paramedic reports the values to the prescriber and the next recheck is set at the provider's interval. Stopping a renoprotective drug for an expected effect, or sending a well patient for same-day evaluation, would both be errors.
factors: Creatinine rise under 25% from a documented baseline
Potassium unchanged
Well, well hydrated, blood pressure at goal
Recheck already planned by the prescriber

followUp.stem: Which result at this recheck would have changed the plan?

options.text: A creatinine more than 50% above baseline
Blood pressure of 126/78, down from 148/90
A creatinine about 15% above the baseline
A potassium of 4.8 mEq/L, up from 4.5

followUp.rationale: A rise over 50% (band 3) or a hyperkalemia would mean the drug is doing harm and needs a same-day decision. A modest rise, a normal potassium and a blood pressure now at goal are the expected picture.

scenarios.title: Steroid leukocytosis on a follow-up CBC

diagnoses: COPD with an exacerbation treated at home last week
baselines: Rose to 13–14 ×10⁹/L during his last prednisone course, with no infection found

visit.reason: Review of a send-out CBC drawn yesterday.
visit.history: Breathing improving, sputum white, no fever, eating well.
visit.vitals: HR 80, BP 134/80, RR 18, SpO2 94% on air (baseline 93–95%), temp 36.8 °C
visit.exam: Scattered wheeze, improving. No focal chest findings.

scenarios.rationale: A steroid-driven leukocytosis of 14 in a COPD patient on prednisone is expected and matches what happened on his last course. He is improving, afebrile, with white sputum. Band 1: a mild leukocytosis alone is weak evidence and is interpreted with the clinical picture, which is good. The prednisone-driven glucose is expected too. Finish the taper and revisit.
factors: Leukocytosis matches his prior steroid response
Afebrile, improving, sputum unchanged
No new focal findings
Course nearly complete

followUp.stem: Which additional finding would make this white cell count meaningful?

options.text: A count of 15.5 ×10⁹/L on the same steroid dose
A fever with a new area of crackles on exam
A fasting glucose of 220 mg/dL on prednisone
The count staying at 13 on the last taper day

followUp.rationale: Infection is read from the patient: fever and a new focal finding. A slightly higher count on steroids, a steroid glucose, or a count persisting through the taper are all consistent with the drug effect.

scenarios.title: Refractory hypokalemia

medications: Potassium chloride 20 mEq twice daily, increased twice in three weeks
baselines: Potassium {kb1} three weeks ago, {kb2} ten days ago, despite each supplement increase

visit.reason: Scheduled potassium recheck.
visit.history: Feels tired, some leg cramps at night. No palpitations, no diarrhea.
visit.vitals: HR 74 regular, BP 122/70, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air
visit.exam: No edema. 12-lead ECG: normal, no U waves.

scenarios.rationale: A potassium that will not rise despite three weeks of escalating supplement, in a patient on a loop diuretic and a long-term proton pump inhibitor, is refractory hypokalemia, and the missing number is magnesium. Potassium cannot be corrected while magnesium is low. Increasing the supplement again is the trap. She is band 1, cramping but with a normal ECG and no arrhythmia, so this is a clinic visit within 24–48 hours for a magnesium level, replacement and a review of the omeprazole, not a same-day problem and not a phone fix.
factors: Potassium unchanged through two supplement increases
Loop diuretic plus PPI: the classic magnesium-depleting pair
Symptomatic (cramps) but ECG normal
Needs a send-out magnesium and a prescription decision

followUp.stem: Which single test is the key to this patient's problem?

options.text: Serum magnesium level
Venous potassium level
24-hour urine potassium
Serum calcium level

followUp.rationale: Refractory hypokalemia is a magnesium problem until proven otherwise. Medics meet magnesium only in eclampsia and torsades and have no framework for chronic depletion in a diuretic-heavy population.

scenarios.title: Aching thighs on a statin

diagnoses: Coronary artery disease, stent two years ago
medications: Atorvastatin 80 mg nightly, increased from 40 mg two months ago

visit.reason: Called the program about aching thighs for three weeks.
visit.history: Symmetrical thigh aching, worse climbing stairs. No dark urine, no fever, no recent fall, no unusual exertion, no injections. Passing urine normally.
visit.vitals: HR 64, BP 128/76, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air
visit.exam: Mild tenderness of both quadriceps, strength 5/5. No swelling.

scenarios.rationale: Symmetrical muscle aching on a recently doubled statin with a CK that has risen from his baseline is statin-associated muscle symptoms. Band 1: ask about exercise, falls and injections, which are excluded here. The right disposition is a clinic visit within 24–48 hours for the prescriber to decide about the dose, not reassurance and not telling him to stop the drug himself. There is no dark urine, no renal change and no weakness, so nothing is emergent.
factors: Clear temporal link to the dose increase
CK risen from a documented baseline
No dark urine, normal creatinine, strength preserved
Prescription decision needed within days

followUp.stem: He asks whether he should just stop the atorvastatin tonight. Best response?

options.text: Yes; stop it and see whether the aching settles
Yes; halve the dose until the clinic visit
No; the prescriber decides, and he has a stent
No; muscle symptoms alone are not a reason to stop

followUp.rationale: Stopping a secondary-prevention statin is a prescriber's decision, made against his coronary history. The paramedic does not change prescriptions, and the symptoms are a real reason for the provider to reconsider the dose.

scenarios.title: HbA1c 12 and a patient who feels fine

social.adherence: Runs out of glimepiride most months before the refill

visit.reason: Clinic asked the program to visit after her HbA1c result.
visit.history: Feels well. Thirstier than usual for months. No vomiting, no weight loss she has noticed.
visit.vitals: HR 80, BP 142/86, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.7 °C
visit.exam: Well hydrated. Feet: intact sensation, no ulcers.

scenarios.rationale: An HbA1c never generates an emergency, and any scenario here with a transport answer is a badly written one. It is a rolling three-month average and cannot answer a question about today; today's glucose is band 1 and the ketones are negative. What it does show is a regimen that is not working, partly because she runs out of glimepiride each month. That needs a clinic visit within 24–48 hours for a regimen change and a refill fix, and the paramedic's contribution is the adherence and supply picture.
factors: HbA1c far above target and rising from last year
Today's glucose only mildly raised, ketones negative
Supply gap identified as a driver
Regimen change is a prescriber decision

followUp.stem: What is the paramedic's most useful contribution before the clinic visit?

options.text: Start a sliding-scale insulin plan at home
Document the refill gap and arrange 90-day supplies
Send a repeat HbA1c to confirm the result
Advise a 1,200-calorie diet until the visit

followUp.rationale: The fixable cause is supply. Insulin and diet plans are the clinic's decisions, and a repeat HbA1c inside three months adds nothing.

scenarios.title: Rising TSH on an unchanged dose

medications: Calcium carbonate 600 mg twice daily, started four months ago
Ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily, started three months ago
baselines: TSH {tshb} six months ago on the same levothyroxine dose

social.adherence: Excellent; takes every pill with breakfast

visit.reason: Review of a TSH result requested by the clinic.
visit.history: More tired, constipated, feels cold. Takes all her morning pills together with breakfast, 'so I don't forget.'
visit.vitals: HR 58, BP 130/80, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air, temp 36.2 °C
visit.exam: Dry skin. Delayed relaxation of ankle reflexes. No goiter. Alert and oriented.

scenarios.rationale: The dose has not changed; what changed is that she now takes calcium and iron with the levothyroxine, and neither lets it absorb. This is a reconciliation and teach-back catch. She is symptomatic but hemodynamically fine, with no hypothermia or altered mentation, so nothing about a TSH is a today decision: a clinic visit within 24–48 hours for the provider to reset the dose and the timing, and the teaching starts now.
factors: Clear timing interaction: calcium and iron taken with the levothyroxine
Symptomatic but stable
Dose decision needs a prescriber
A recheck will take six weeks to reflect any change

followUp.stem: What should she be taught about taking her morning pills?

options.text: Take the levothyroxine with the calcium, for routine
Take the levothyroxine alone, hours apart from the rest
Stop the calcium and iron; the thyroid matters more
Double the levothyroxine on days she takes the iron

followUp.rationale: Separation by several hours restores absorption. Stopping the supplements or self-adjusting the dose are not the paramedic's or the patient's call.

scenarios.title: Drifting hemoglobin on two NSAIDs

medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily, bought over the counter

visit.reason: Routine visit; reports feeling 'a bit washed out.'
visit.history: No black or bloody stools, no vomiting, no abdominal pain, no chest pain or breathlessness. Takes ibuprofen daily for her knees.
visit.vitals: HR 78, BP 134/80, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air. Orthostatic vitals normal.
visit.exam: Pale conjunctivae. Abdomen soft, non-tender. No melena on history.

scenarios.rationale: The hemoglobin is only band 1, but it is drifting down from a documented value on two drugs that cause GI blood loss, and she is symptomatic. Feeling well is not a laboratory finding. There is no melena, no hemodynamic change and normal orthostatics, so nothing is emergent, but this needs a clinic work-up within 24–48 hours for occult loss and a decision about the ibuprofen. Absolute value alone could not have separated this from a stable chronic anemia; the baseline and the medication list did.
factors: Fall from a documented baseline on aspirin plus daily NSAID
Symptomatic but hemodynamically normal
No melena or active bleeding
Prescriber decision needed on the NSAID

followUp.stem: Which finding on this visit would have made the disposition emergent?

options.text: A hemoglobin of 10.4 g/dL instead of today's
Black, tarry stools for the past two days
Pale conjunctivae and nail beds on exam
Ibuprofen use for six months rather than four

followUp.rationale: Melena is the table's trigger: any level with frank bleeding is emergent. A slightly lower number, pallor or a longer NSAID history change the urgency of the work-up, not the tier.

scenarios.title: Digoxin level just over the line

baselines: Digoxin {digb} a year ago, drawn 8 hours post-dose

visit.reason: Review of an annual digoxin level.
visit.history: Feels her usual self. Eating normally, no nausea, no visual disturbance, no confusion.
visit.vitals: HR 66 irregular, BP 128/74, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air
visit.exam: Alert. 12-lead ECG: atrial fibrillation, rate controlled, no new changes.

scenarios.rationale: A correctly timed level just above the reference range in a patient with no symptoms, a normal potassium, a stable creatinine and an unchanged ECG is band 1: a provider consult on dose reduction, which in practice means a clinic review within 24–48 hours. The electrolytes and renal function matter more than the level itself, and they are fine. Nausea, visual change, confusion or new bradycardia would make it urgent.
factors: Level mildly above range and correctly timed
No toxicity symptoms, ECG unchanged
Potassium and creatinine normal and stable
Dose reduction is a prescriber decision

followUp.stem: Which change since last year most plausibly explains the higher level?

options.text: A gradual decline in kidney function
The daughter now fills the pill organizer
Warfarin dose changes over the year
A draw at nine instead of eight hours

followUp.rationale: Digoxin accumulates as renal clearance falls, even when a single creatinine still looks acceptable. Warfarin does not change digoxin levels, organized dosing would not raise it, and an extra hour post-dose would lower, not raise, the reading.

scenarios.title: Fatigue, low ferritin, and a question about the source

patient.goals: Full treatment; overdue for colon cancer screening by her own account

visit.reason: Review of send-out results drawn for fatigue.
visit.history: Tired for three months. Post-menopausal, no vaginal bleeding. No melena or visible blood. No NSAID use. Eats meat.
visit.vitals: HR 82, BP 130/78, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air
visit.exam: Pale. Abdomen soft, non-tender.

scenarios.rationale: None of the hematinics produce an emergency, and she is hemodynamically well with no active bleeding. But a new iron deficiency in a post-menopausal woman who eats meat and takes no NSAIDs is occult GI loss until proven otherwise, and the fall from her prior hemoglobin says it is real. That needs a clinic visit within 24–48 hours to start iron and, more importantly, to arrange the source work-up she is already overdue for. Replacement alone without a source search would be the error.
factors: New iron deficiency with a falling hemoglobin
No dietary or NSAID explanation
Post-menopausal: GI source until excluded
Overdue for screening

followUp.stem: What is the most important thing the clinic visit must arrange?

options.text: A source work-up, starting with the GI tract
A repeat ferritin after a month of iron
A transfusion to correct the hemoglobin
A switch from lisinopril to a different drug

followUp.rationale: Iron deficiency in this patient is a finding, not a diagnosis. Replacing iron treats the number; the source is what matters.

scenarios.title: Falls and a low vitamin D

patient.living: Housebound in an apartment; rarely outdoors since his wife died.
baselines: Vitamin D never checked before this draw

social.support: Meals delivered; home health aide twice weekly
social.mobility: Furniture-walks indoors; two falls in three months, no injury

patient.goals: Wants to stay in his apartment

visit.reason: Falls assessment; send-out results reviewed.
visit.history: Two falls getting up from his chair, no dizziness, no injury. Eats little. Rarely in daylight. Nocturia twice a night.
visit.vitals: HR 70, BP 134/78 lying, 128/76 standing, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air
visit.exam: Proximal leg weakness rising from the chair. Slow gait. No focal deficit.

scenarios.rationale: A housebound, bereaved older man with proximal weakness, poor intake and a low vitamin D is the classic bundled case. Nothing about the number is urgent and it cannot produce a transport answer. But the falls are recurrent and multifactorial: the vitamin D, the tamsulosin and nocturia, the low mood, the furniture-walking. That is a clinic visit within 24–48 hours for replacement, a medication review and a physical therapy referral, with the paramedic setting up the home side now.
factors: Recurrent falls with proximal weakness
Vitamin D deficiency in a housebound patient
Alpha-blocker and nocturia as contributing factors
Low mood since bereavement

followUp.stem: Which referral can the paramedic make today without a provider order?

options.text: Physical therapy for strength and balance
An orthopedic consultation about his hips
A prescription vitamin D loading dose
A change of tamsulosin to a different drug

followUp.rationale: Under the program protocol the paramedic can arrange home health and therapy referrals directly. Prescriptions and specialist consults go through the provider.

scenarios.title: INR of six with no bleeding

medications: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, course finished six days ago
baselines: INR {inrb} a month ago, on the same warfarin dose
No prior INR above 3.2 in two years of records

visit.reason: Scheduled INR check after the antibiotic course.
visit.history: No bleeding, bruising, black stools, hematuria, falls or head injury. Urinary symptoms resolved.
visit.vitals: HR 70 irregular, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air
visit.exam: No bruising, no petechiae, no oral bleeding. Abdomen soft. Neurologically normal.

scenarios.rationale: An INR of 4.5–9.0 without bleeding means hold the dose, not call an ambulance. The antibiotic explains it: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole raises the INR and a course finished last week still counts. Band 2: hold warfarin on a provider phone order, oral vitamin K if the provider chooses, and a recheck within 24–48 hours, which here is a clinic or return visit. A paramedic's binary training offers no middle option and defaults to transport; the correct answer sits in the middle.
factors: Supratherapeutic with no bleeding, no falls, no head injury
Clear drug interaction with a finished antibiotic
Hold and recheck available by phone order
Reliable patient with a spouse at home

followUp.stem: What should the paramedic tell the couple to watch for before the recheck?

options.text: A fall, head strike, black stools, or bleeding
Dizziness on standing or a racing heartbeat
New swelling or pain in one calf or thigh
A fever or a return of the urinary symptoms

followUp.rationale: At this INR the risk is bleeding, and a head injury on anticoagulation goes in regardless of the number. The other symptoms are worth knowing but are not the specific danger of a high INR.

scenarios.title: Two potassium-raising drugs and a supplement

medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily, started last week for her knee
Potassium supplement from the pharmacy shelf, started last week 'for cramps'

social.adherence: Good; adds over-the-counter products without asking

visit.reason: Routine visit; new over-the-counter products noted on the medication check.
visit.history: Feels well apart from the knee. No palpitations, weakness or numbness.
visit.vitals: HR 70 regular, BP 138/82, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air
visit.exam: Well. 12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm, no peaked T waves, QRS 90 ms.

scenarios.rationale: An ACE inhibitor, a new NSAID, a potassium supplement and reduced GFR: any two of these together is the table's named danger combination, and she has all four. The potassium has climbed more than a full mEq/L in two months. Band 2 is same-day evaluation with an ECG, and the ECG is normal today, so this is not emergent; but it is not a phone fix either, because the number is still climbing and she needs a repeat and a plan the same day. Stopping the supplement and the ibuprofen is part of the plan, not a substitute for the evaluation.
factors: Four potassium-raising factors together
Rise of more than 1 mEq/L from baseline
ECG normal today
Son can drive her to the clinic now

followUp.stem: Which ECG change would have made this an emergent transport?

options.text: Peaked T waves with a widening QRS
Sinus bradycardia at a rate of 58
A first-degree AV block, PR 220 ms
Left axis deviation on the 12-lead

followUp.rationale: Any level with ECG change of hyperkalemia is band 3. Peaked T waves and QRS widening are the changes to look for; the others are not features of hyperkalemia.

scenarios.title: Positive D-dimer, moderate pretest

visit.reason: Review of a send-out D-dimer drawn yesterday for a week of right calf ache after a 14-hour drive.
visit.history: Calf ache, no chest pain, no breathlessness, no hemoptysis, no syncope. No prior clot, no cancer, no surgery.
visit.vitals: HR 84, BP 138/84, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.8 °C
visit.exam: Right calf 2 cm larger than the left, mildly tender, no erythema. Chest clear.

scenarios.rationale: Moderate pretest probability with a positive D-dimer needs imaging, so a same-day referral for a leg ultrasound; on its own the result diagnoses nothing. He has no chest symptoms, no hypoxia and normal vitals, so there is no case for emergent transport, and a positive D-dimer becoming an automatic ambulance ride is exactly the reflex this scenario targets. Dismissing it because D-dimer is nonspecific would be the opposite error.
factors: Moderate pretest probability: travel, unilateral swelling
Positive D-dimer requires imaging to rule in or out
No chest symptoms, no hypoxia, normal vitals
Private transport available today

followUp.stem: Which additional finding would have changed this to emergent transport?

options.text: A D-dimer result of 2,500 ng/mL FEU
Calf circumference difference of 3 cm
New pleuritic chest pain with SpO2 of 91%
A 20-hour drive instead of a 14-hour one

followUp.rationale: Hypoxia, syncope, unilateral leg swelling with chest symptoms, or high pretest probability make it band 3 regardless of the number. A higher D-dimer, a bigger calf, or a longer drive raise the probability but not the tier on their own.

scenarios.title: New thiazide, falling sodium

medications: Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, started five days ago
baselines: Sodium {nab} on the panel drawn the day the thiazide was started

social.cognition: Intact at baseline; manages her own pills

visit.reason: Family called: 'she seems muddled since the new pill.'
visit.history: Mildly forgetful and unsteady for two days. Nauseated, eating less. No headache, no vomiting, no seizure, no falls.
visit.vitals: HR 78, BP 128/76, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.7 °C
visit.exam: Oriented to person and place, not to date; her family say this is new. Gait mildly unsteady. No focal deficit.

scenarios.rationale: The same number as the stable heart-failure patient, but this sodium has fallen from 140 in five days on a new thiazide, and she is symptomatic: new mild confusion, nausea, unsteadiness. That is an acute change, band 2 at minimum, and it needs same-day evaluation and a decision about the drug today. Marked confusion, seizure or a focal deficit would make it emergent; she has none of those, and the family can take her.
factors: Fall of about 12 mEq/L in five days
New symptoms attributable to the sodium
Clear cause: new thiazide
No seizure, no marked confusion, no focal deficit

followUp.stem: What should the paramedic do about the hydrochlorothiazide right now?

options.text: Tell her to stop it for good on her own
Ask the provider by phone whether to hold it
Continue it and let the clinic decide
Halve the dose until the clinic visit

followUp.rationale: Holding a medication is a provider order under the protocol; the paramedic does not stop or adjust it independently. Continuing a drug that is causing symptomatic hyponatremia until someone else decides is not acceptable either.

scenarios.title: Creatinine doubled after contrast and ibuprofen

diagnoses: Discharged four days ago after a CT pulmonary angiogram (negative)
medications: Ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily since discharge

visit.reason: Post-discharge visit.
visit.history: Feels 'washed out.' Passing urine, volume seems a little less. No chest pain, no breathlessness, no vomiting.
visit.vitals: HR 80, BP 142/84, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.8 °C
visit.exam: Mildly dry mucous membranes. No edema. Lungs clear.

scenarios.rationale: Creatinine more than 50% above his admission baseline after contrast, an NSAID and an ACE inhibitor together: band 3 on the table, which reads 'urgent or emergent.' What decides between the two is the rest of the picture: he is making urine, his potassium is normal, he is not overloaded and not hypotensive. That is same-day evaluation with the family driving, and the NSAID stops on a provider order now. Oliguria, hyperkalemia or hypotension would make it emergent.
factors: Creatinine rise over 50% from a documented baseline
Three nephrotoxic exposures in one week
Still passing urine; potassium normal; hemodynamically stable
Same-day labs and a fluid plan needed

followUp.stem: Which medication should the paramedic ask the provider about holding today?

options.text: Amlodipine and lisinopril
Ibuprofen and lisinopril
Ibuprofen and amlodipine
None until the clinic decides

followUp.rationale: Both the NSAID and the ACE inhibitor reduce glomerular perfusion in an acute kidney injury; the provider will usually hold both until the creatinine recovers. Amlodipine is not nephrotoxic.

scenarios.title: Sick-day insulin cut and moderate ketones

medications: Insulin lispro with meals per carbohydrate count

social.adherence: Good; has never been taught sick-day rules

visit.reason: Called the program: high readings for two days with a cold.
visit.history: Cut her glargine to 12 units because she was 'not eating much.' Drinking fluids, not vomiting, no abdominal pain. Breathing normally.
visit.vitals: HR 92, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 98% on air, temp 37.6 °C
visit.exam: Alert, mildly dry lips. No Kussmaul breathing, no acetone smell. Abdomen soft.

scenarios.rationale: Moderate urine ketones with a glucose above 250 in a type 1 diabetic who has cut her basal insulin during illness is band 2: same-day evaluation, because this needs a bicarbonate and an insulin plan today, and a paramedic cannot provide either at the kitchen table. She is alert, not vomiting, breathing normally and drinking, so it is not yet emergent. Reducing insulin during illness is the error that produced the picture; requirements rise with illness.
factors: Moderate ketonuria with glucose over 250
Basal insulin reduced during an illness
Alert, drinking, not vomiting, no Kussmaul breathing
Needs a bicarbonate and an insulin plan today

followUp.stem: Which finding would move her to emergent transport?

options.text: A glucose reading climbing above 350 mg/dL
Ketones rising to large, with vomiting
A temperature of 38.2 °C this afternoon
Not eating anything for the rest of the day

followUp.rationale: Large ketones, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing, altered mentation or a low bicarbonate are band 3. A higher glucose, a modest fever or reduced intake raise the concern without changing the tier on their own.

scenarios.title: Platelets halved on new heparin

patient.living: Lives with her husband; discharged after a hip repair eight days ago.

visit.reason: Review of a send-out CBC drawn yesterday by home health.
visit.history: Wound healing. No bleeding, bruising is limited to injection sites. No new leg swelling, no chest symptoms.
visit.vitals: HR 82, BP 134/80, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.9 °C
visit.exam: Wound clean. Calves soft, non-tender. Small injection-site bruises.

scenarios.rationale: The number is only band 1, but it has roughly halved from her pre-operative baseline between days five and ten of a heparin product, which is exactly the window for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. That is a same-day decision about stopping the enoxaparin and switching anticoagulant, because HIT causes clots, not bleeding, and she is a post-operative patient who needs prophylaxis. She has no bleeding and no new thrombosis, so it is not emergent; it cannot wait 48 hours either.
factors: Platelets fell by half on days 5–10 of heparin exposure
No bleeding; risk is thrombosis
Anticoagulant change is a same-day prescriber decision
Husband can drive her today

followUp.stem: Until she is seen, what should the paramedic advise about the enoxaparin?

options.text: Give tonight's dose exactly as usual
Ask the provider now about holding it
Halve tonight's dose as a precaution
Switch to aspirin from the cabinet

followUp.rationale: A suspected HIT needs the heparin stopped, but that and its replacement are prescriber decisions the paramedic obtains by phone now, not by improvising.

scenarios.title: Three kilograms and three pillows

diagnoses: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
baselines: Dry weight 68 kg; BNP {bnpb} at dry weight three months ago

visit.reason: Daughter called about ankle swelling and a weight jump.
visit.history: Weight up 3 kg over four days. Now sleeping on three pillows; woke breathless once last night. Took the furosemide every day. Ate a salty restaurant meal on Sunday.
visit.vitals: HR 88 irregular, BP 138/84, RR 20, SpO2 94% on air (usual 96–97%), temp 36.7 °C, weight 71 kg
visit.exam: Raised jugular venous pressure. Bibasal crackles. Pitting edema to mid-shin. Speaks full sentences.

scenarios.rationale: This is decompensation, and the weight told you before the BNP did: 3 kg in four days against a known dry weight, new orthopnea, crackles and a raised JVP. The BNP is band 2 and several times her dry-weight baseline, which confirms the trend. She is speaking full sentences with a saturation of 94% and no hypotension, so it is not emergent; but it needs a same-day diuretic decision, and a phone consult alone would leave her at home with a chest that is filling. Resting hypoxia, orthopnea at rest or hypotension would make it band 3.
factors: 3 kg over dry weight in four days with new orthopnea
Exam confirms congestion: JVP, crackles, edema
BNP several times her documented baseline
No resting hypoxia, no hypotension; conversational

followUp.stem: Which measure best tracks whether the treatment is working over the following week?

options.text: A repeat BNP drawn on each visit
Daily weight against her dry weight
Daily oxygen saturation readings
The number of pillows she sleeps on

followUp.rationale: Daily weights beat a single BNP for detecting and tracking decompensation. BNP lags and varies; saturation and pillow count are late signs.

scenarios.title: Toxic on a therapeutic level

medications: Furosemide 40 mg daily, started at discharge two weeks ago

visit.reason: Daughter called: nausea, not eating, 'seeing things yellow.'
visit.history: Three days of nausea, poor appetite and a yellow tint to her vision. Mildly confused this morning per the daughter. No chest pain, no syncope.
visit.vitals: HR 48 irregular, BP 118/70, RR 14, SpO2 96% on air, temp 36.6 °C
visit.exam: Alert, oriented to person and place. 12-lead ECG: atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response, no other acute change.

scenarios.rationale: A digoxin level inside the reference range does not exclude toxicity. Since discharge she has started a loop diuretic, her potassium has fallen and her creatinine has risen, and all three potentiate the drug; nausea, anorexia, yellow vision and a new slow rate are the classic presentation. Band 2 on the table: urgent evaluation, and symptoms outrank the number. She is alert with a maintained blood pressure and no syncope, so same-day evaluation with the daughter driving rather than an ambulance; a symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension, an arrhythmia or significant hyperkalemia would make it emergent. The digoxin is held on a phone order now.
factors: Classic toxicity symptoms despite an in-range level
New loop diuretic with hypokalemia and a rising creatinine
Bradycardia without hypotension or syncope
Level on file is two weeks old

followUp.stem: Which lab changes since discharge most explain her toxicity?

options.text: Falling potassium and rising creatinine
An INR drifting above the target range
A higher digoxin level than at discharge
A raised BNP from her heart failure

followUp.rationale: Hypokalemia potentiates digoxin at the receptor and reduced clearance raises the effective exposure, so a patient can be toxic at a level that looks fine. The INR and BNP are unrelated, and the level on file is two weeks old.

scenarios.title: Refeeding on day two

patient.living: Lives alone; discharged two days ago after a week of eating almost nothing.
diagnoses: Alcohol use disorder, abstinent since admission
medications: Oral nutrition supplement three times daily

social.transport: None; program can arrange scheduled transport today

patient.goals: Full treatment; motivated to stay abstinent

visit.reason: Post-discharge visit; send-out phosphate from this morning reported by phone.
visit.history: Eating three full meals plus supplements since discharge. Now weak, 'legs like jelly,' mild tingling around the mouth. No chest pain, no breathlessness at rest.
visit.vitals: HR 96, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.8 °C
visit.exam: Proximal weakness, rises from chair with arms. No edema. 12-lead ECG: sinus tachycardia, no arrhythmia.

scenarios.rationale: A malnourished patient restarted on full nutrition can drop his phosphate sharply in the first 24–72 hours, and the paramedic doing the day-two visit is positioned to catch it. The phosphate has halved from discharge, the potassium is falling too, and he is symptomatic with weakness and perioral tingling. Band 2 is a provider consult, but with symptoms and two falling electrolytes this is a same-day evaluation for replacement and a slower feeding plan, not a phone call. Respiratory weakness or an arrhythmia would make it emergent.
factors: Phosphate halved since discharge on full refeeding
Potassium also falling
Symptomatic: weakness, perioral tingling
No respiratory compromise or arrhythmia yet

followUp.stem: Before the evaluation, what should he be told about the supplement drinks?

options.text: Stop them entirely until he has been seen
Pause them until seen, on the provider's advice
Continue them exactly as prescribed for now
Double them to rebuild his strength faster

followUp.rationale: The refeeding load is the problem, so the provider will usually pause the calorie push until electrolytes are replaced; that instruction comes from the provider, not the paramedic, and 'stop entirely' without a plan risks the opposite error.

scenarios.title: Hemoglobin down four grams in a month

diagnoses: Prior peptic ulcer, twenty years ago
medications: Naproxen 500 mg twice daily, daily for two months

visit.reason: Reports being 'more tired than usual' for two weeks.
visit.history: No black stools he has noticed, no vomiting, no chest pain. Breathless carrying groceries, new. Takes naproxen every day.
visit.vitals: HR 96, BP 128/76 lying, 118/72 standing, RR 16, SpO2 97% on air
visit.exam: Pale. Abdomen soft, mild epigastric tenderness. No melena on history; no rectal exam performed.

scenarios.rationale: A fall of about four grams in a month on a daily NSAID in a man with an ulcer history is an occult bleed until proven otherwise. Band 2 with a recent fall: urgent, look for a source. He is tachycardic and mildly orthostatic but not hypotensive, not actively bleeding and not syncopal, so this is same-day evaluation with the wife driving, not an ambulance; melena, hematemesis or hemodynamic compromise would make it emergent. The same 9.5 in a CKD patient stable for eighteen months would have been a trend-it number.
factors: Four-gram fall from a documented baseline in a month
Daily NSAID with an ulcer history
Symptomatic, tachycardic, mildly orthostatic, not hypotensive
No visible bleeding or melena

followUp.stem: What should the paramedic do about the naproxen before he is seen?

options.text: Ask the provider now for an order to hold it
Continue it so the clinic sees the true picture
Replace it with ibuprofen, which is gentler
Tell him to take it only with food from now on

followUp.rationale: The likely source of the bleeding is the NSAID, and holding it is a provider order the paramedic obtains by phone. Swapping to another NSAID or adding food does not remove the risk.

scenarios.title: Fever after chemotherapy

diagnoses: Breast cancer on adjuvant chemotherapy, cycle 3 given ten days ago
baselines: White cell count {wbcb} before this cycle
Oncology instructions on file: 'call for any temperature of 38.0 °C or above'

social.transport: Husband can drive; oncology center 50 minutes away

visit.reason: Husband called: temperature 38.3 °C at home, 'she seems fine.'
visit.history: Felt 'a bit off' since last night. No cough, no dysuria, no sore throat, no diarrhea. Port site clean.
visit.vitals: HR 104, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 97% on air, temp 38.3 °C
visit.exam: Looks well. Port site clean, no erythema. Chest clear. Abdomen soft. No mucositis.

labs.label: White cell count (send-out drawn yesterday by home health, reported this morning)

scenarios.rationale: Neutropenic fever: a temperature of 38.3 °C ten days after chemotherapy with a white cell count under 1.0, which means an absolute neutrophil count far below 500. Band 3, emergent transport, because the antibiotic window is narrow and the patient often looks entirely well. The normal lactate, the clean port and the clear chest are reassuring about where the infection is, not about whether it is there. Medics have essentially no exposure to this, and the instinct to reassure and leave is exactly wrong.
factors: Fever in the neutropenic window after chemotherapy
White cell count under 1.0 ×10⁹/L
Well appearance is expected and does not lower the tier
Time to antibiotics matters

followUp.stem: Which action is correct while awaiting transport?

options.text: Give acetaminophen and recheck the temperature
Draw blood cultures from the port before antibiotics
Call ahead so antibiotics are ready on arrival
Start the oral antibiotic from the vehicle kit

followUp.rationale: Pre-notification shortens time to antibiotics, which is the outcome that matters. Antipyretics mask the fever without treating it, port cultures are the receiving team's job, and an oral kit antibiotic is not adequate for neutropenic fever.

scenarios.title: The long lie

patient.living: Lives alone; pendant alarm not worn at night.
patient.goals: Full treatment; wants to stay at home

visit.reason: Referred by the responding crew after a fall; she declined transport this morning and asked for a home visit.
visit.history: Fell at about 10 pm going to the bathroom, could not get up, found by the neighbor at 8 am. Cold, stiff, now sitting comfortably. Has passed a small amount of dark urine.
visit.vitals: HR 88, BP 132/78, RR 16, SpO2 96% on air, temp 36.4 °C
visit.exam: Bruising over the right hip and shoulder, full range of motion, no bony tenderness. Thigh muscles tender. Alert and oriented.

labs.label: CK (send-out drawn by the morning crew, called through)

scenarios.rationale: Ten hours on the floor, dark urine, a CK in the thousands, a creatinine already 30–40% above her baseline and a potassium starting to climb: this is rhabdomyolysis with evolving kidney injury, band 3 on the table, and the fact that she is now sitting comfortably in a chair is exactly why the table says the number should override a reassuring exam. She declined once; the visit is the chance to explain why this goes in now. The metformin is held.
factors: Prolonged down time with dark urine
CK far above 5000 U/L
Creatinine rising and potassium climbing
Comfortable appearance is misleading

followUp.stem: She asks why she needs to go now when she 'feels fine sitting here.' The best explanation is that:

options.text: The bruising may hide a hip fracture that needs X-ray
Muscle breakdown is damaging her kidneys and needs IV fluids now
Her potassium means her heart could stop at any moment
She needs observation overnight because she lives alone

followUp.rationale: Honest and specific: the CK and creatinine show muscle breakdown injuring the kidneys, and the treatment is aggressive IV fluids she cannot get at home. The potassium is not yet dangerous, the hip exam is reassuring, and living alone is a discharge-planning issue, not the reason for transport.

scenarios.title: Negative D-dimer, wrong question

patient.living: Lives with his wife; discharged two weeks ago after a hip replacement.
diagnoses: Right hip replacement, two weeks ago
medications: Aspirin 81 mg twice daily (post-operative prophylaxis, prescribed for 4 weeks)

visit.reason: Home health drew a D-dimer yesterday for a swollen calf and asked the program to review it.
visit.history: Left calf swollen and tender for three days. Since this morning, short of breath walking to the bathroom and a sharp pain on the left when breathing in. No cough, no fever.
visit.vitals: HR 112, BP 126/78, RR 22, SpO2 90% on air, temp 37.2 °C
visit.exam: Left calf 3 cm larger than the right, tender. Chest clear to auscultation. Speaks in short sentences.

scenarios.rationale: Recent major orthopedic surgery, unilateral leg swelling, new pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia: high pretest probability. A negative D-dimer does not exclude pulmonary embolism when the pretest probability is high, and ordering one in that setting was the wrong test, because a negative result could never have changed anything. Band 3, emergent transport. The single most instructive D-dimer scenario: the number is the least important thing on the page.
factors: High pretest probability: recent surgery, unilateral swelling, pleuritic pain
New hypoxia and tachycardia
Negative D-dimer carries no weight at this probability
Deteriorating since the sample was drawn

followUp.stem: In which patient would a negative D-dimer have been genuinely useful?

options.text: This patient, before the chest pain had begun
Pleuritic pain, normal vitals, no risk factors
A known cancer and a newly swollen leg
Syncope with a resting heart rate of 120

followUp.rationale: A D-dimer has clinical meaning only as a rule-out, and only when pretest probability is low or moderate. Recent surgery, cancer, syncope with tachycardia, or unilateral swelling all push the probability too high for a negative result to matter.

scenarios.title: Lactate that contradicts the exam

visit.reason: Son called about two days of burning on urination and a low fever; asked for antibiotics at home.
visit.history: Dysuria and frequency for two days, chills last night. Eating and drinking. No flank pain, no vomiting. Feels 'a bit tired.'
visit.vitals: HR 92, BP 128/74, RR 18, SpO2 96% on air, temp 38.1 °C
visit.exam: Looks comfortable. Mild suprapubic tenderness, no flank tenderness. Skin warm and dry. Alert.

scenarios.rationale: On appearance alone she is a cystitis with a fever, and the son's request for antibiotics at home is reasonable on the face of it. The lactate says otherwise: over 4 mmol/L with an infective source is Sepsis-3 territory and carries markedly increased mortality regardless of how well she looks. This is the value that most often contradicts the physical exam, and that is precisely its worth. Emergent transport; the metformin is held because of the lactate and the illness.
factors: Lactate over 4 mmol/L with a fever and an infective source
Vitals and appearance are falsely reassuring
Diabetic on metformin: additional reason to hold the drug
Early sepsis has the best outcomes when treated early

followUp.stem: Which medication should be held on transport, and why?

options.text: Amlodipine, because sepsis will lower her pressure
Metformin, because of the lactate and the illness
Nitrofurantoin, because it bred a resistant organism
None of them; the hospital will review the list

followUp.rationale: Metformin is held during any acute illness that threatens perfusion because the risk is lactic acidosis, and her lactate is already high. Nitrofurantoin was stopped last month; amlodipine is a hospital decision.

scenarios.title: Head strike on warfarin

visit.reason: Daughter called: her mother slipped in the kitchen an hour ago and hit her head on the counter.
visit.history: No loss of consciousness, remembers the fall. Mild headache. No vomiting, no visual change. Wants to 'just put ice on it.'
visit.vitals: HR 72 irregular, BP 146/82, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air
visit.exam: 2 cm scalp bruise over the right parietal area, no laceration. Pupils equal and reactive. Neurological exam normal. Oriented.

scenarios.rationale: Band 3 by definition: any head injury on anticoagulation goes in for imaging even with a therapeutic number and a normal exam. Intracranial bleeding on warfarin can be delayed, and a normal exam an hour after the fall proves nothing. The therapeutic INR is the trap; a medic who reads 2.5 as 'safe' has misunderstood what the number is for.
factors: Head strike while anticoagulated
Normal exam and therapeutic INR do not exclude bleeding
Delayed intracranial hemorrhage is the specific risk
Imaging is the only way to clear her

followUp.stem: Which INR result would have changed this disposition?

options.text: An INR of 1.4
An INR of 3.6
None of them
An INR of 0.9

followUp.rationale: A head injury on warfarin goes in regardless of the INR. A subtherapeutic number reduces the risk but does not remove it, and a supratherapeutic one only raises the urgency.

scenarios.title: Acute on chronic

patient.living: Lives with his wife; home oxygen 1.5 L/min.
diagnoses: Severe COPD with chronic CO2 retention
Obstructive sleep apnea, does not use CPAP
medications: Zolpidem 5 mg nightly, started by an out-of-hours service last week for poor sleep
baselines: Venous gas three months ago: pH {phb}, pCO2 {pco2b}, bicarbonate {hco3b}
Usual SpO2 89–91% on 1.5 L/min; usual mentation alert
patient.goals: Full treatment; has previously accepted non-invasive ventilation

visit.reason: Wife called: 'he has been very sleepy since yesterday.'
visit.history: More breathless for three days, sputum yellower. Drowsy since last evening, hard to wake this morning. Took the zolpidem the past four nights.
visit.vitals: HR 102, BP 148/88, RR 24 shallow, SpO2 86% on 1.5 L/min, temp 37.4 °C
visit.exam: Drowsy, rousable to voice, drifts off. Flapping tremor present. Reduced air entry, wheeze. Using accessory muscles.

scenarios.rationale: His baseline gas is compensated; this one is not. The bicarbonate has not moved, the pCO2 has risen well past his usual and the pH has fallen below 7.30, with new drowsiness, asterixis and accessory muscle use: acute-on-chronic respiratory failure, band 3, emergent transport, and he has previously accepted non-invasive ventilation. The word 'retainer' in the history is the trap; the gas says acute. The new zolpidem is the likely precipitant on top of an exacerbation.
factors: pH under 7.30 with pCO2 far above his documented baseline
Bicarbonate unchanged: no time to compensate, therefore acute
Falling mentation and asterixis
New sedative on top of an exacerbation

followUp.stem: Which medication on his list most likely tipped him over?

options.text: Tiotropium
Budesonide-formoterol
Zolpidem
Albuterol

followUp.rationale: A sedative-hypnotic in a CO2 retainer with untreated sleep apnea suppresses ventilation and is a classic precipitant. The inhalers are treatment, not cause.

scenarios.title: Pump failure and Kussmaul breathing

diagnoses: Type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump
baselines: One prior admission for ketoacidosis three years ago

visit.reason: Partner called: vomiting since 5 am, pump 'was showing an occlusion alarm' overnight.
visit.history: Nausea and vomiting for four hours, abdominal pain, very thirsty. Pump site dislodged. No insulin delivered for at least eight hours.
visit.vitals: HR 118, BP 108/66, RR 26 deep, SpO2 98% on air, temp 37.0 °C
visit.exam: Drowsy but answering. Deep, rapid breathing with a fruity odor. Dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor. Abdomen diffusely tender, soft.

scenarios.rationale: Diabetic ketoacidosis after eight hours without insulin: glucose over 400, large urine ketones, bicarbonate under 15, Kussmaul breathing, vomiting and drowsiness. Every one of those is band 3 on its own; together there is no decision to make except how fast. The pump is the mechanism, not the treatment; he needs IV insulin, fluids and potassium management in hospital. The potassium looks high now and will fall sharply with treatment, which is the receiving team's problem to anticipate.
factors: No insulin delivery for eight hours in type 1 diabetes
Large ketones with a low bicarbonate: acidosis, not just hyperglycemia
Kussmaul breathing, vomiting, dehydration, drowsiness
Tachycardic with a soft blood pressure

followUp.stem: Which action is correct before the ambulance arrives?

options.text: Give a correction bolus through the pump
Give a subcutaneous dose from his pen as a bridge
Encourage him to drink two liters of water
Reattach the pump site and restart the basal rate

followUp.rationale: Once the pump has failed, a subcutaneous dose from a backup pen per his own sick-day plan is the accepted bridge; a bolus through a failed pump or a re-sited pump cannot be trusted, and oral water will not fix the acidosis in a vomiting patient. Any dose is given per his plan or a provider order, and transport is not delayed for it.

scenarios.title: Cirrhosis, somnolent, cannot swallow

baselines: Ammonia {nh3b} last month when oriented and walking

visit.reason: Brother called: 'I can't keep him awake.'
visit.history: Increasingly sleepy since yesterday, vomited once this morning, could not swallow his lactulose. Two dark stools yesterday per the brother. Taking all medications until today.
visit.vitals: HR 104, BP 102/60, RR 16, SpO2 95% on air, temp 37.1 °C
visit.exam: Somnolent, rousable to sternal rub, not oriented. Asterixis. Abdomen distended, non-tender. Pale.

labs.label: Ammonia (send-out from yesterday's clinic draw, reported this morning)

scenarios.rationale: The ammonia is barely above his baseline, and a medic who reads the number would be reassured. The patient is somnolent, cannot take oral lactulose, has dark stools and a falling hemoglobin with a soft blood pressure in a man with banded varices. Band 3 is defined clinically: marked confusion, somnolence, inability to take lactulose, or evidence of GI bleeding, and he has all four. A cirrhotic at 90 who is oriented does not need an ambulance; one at 70 who has become somnolent does.
factors: Somnolence: grade 3 encephalopathy
Cannot take oral lactulose
Dark stools, falling hemoglobin, tachycardia, soft pressure: possible variceal bleed
Ammonia level is irrelevant to the decision

followUp.stem: Which finding makes this more than an encephalopathy problem?

options.text: The asterixis found on examination
The ammonia above his baseline
Dark stools with a falling hemoglobin
The distended, non-tender abdomen

followUp.rationale: GI bleeding is both a precipitant of encephalopathy and an emergency in its own right in a patient with varices. Asterixis and ascites are expected in his disease; the ammonia does not decide anything.

scenarios.title: An old troponin and a new chest pain

diagnoses: NSTEMI two weeks ago, treated with a stent
baselines: Discharge summary lists a peak troponin of {tropb}; no troponin drawn since
Discharge ECG on file: resolved ST changes, Q waves in leads III and aVF
Prior troponin before the event: none on record

social.mobility: Independent; cardiac rehab starts next week

visit.reason: Scheduled post-discharge visit.
visit.history: On arrival he mentions 20 minutes of central chest pressure while carrying laundry an hour ago, eased with rest; 'the same feeling as before.' Now mild residual discomfort. No breathlessness, no syncope.
visit.vitals: HR 78, BP 134/80, RR 16, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.7 °C
visit.exam: Looks anxious, otherwise well. Chest clear. 12-lead ECG: new T-wave inversion in leads V4–V6 compared with the discharge tracing.

scenarios.rationale: The troponin on the discharge sheet is a historical peak from an event already treated, and it tells you nothing about today; the infarct is not re-decided in someone's living room. What decides today is the history and the ECG: exertional chest pressure that he recognizes, two weeks after a stent, with new T-wave inversion compared with his discharge tracing. That is band 3 for troponin's row, a new event with chest pain and an ECG change, and no number is needed to make the call. Emergent transport, aspirin already on board, nitroglycerin per protocol.
factors: Recognizable exertional chest pain two weeks after a stent
New ECG change against the discharge tracing
Discharge troponin is irrelevant to today's decision
Stent thrombosis is a time-critical possibility

followUp.stem: What is the correct use of the discharge troponin value today?

options.text: Compare it with a point-of-care troponin today
Gauge the size of the recent event; nothing more
Use it as his baseline for the receiving team
Ignore it, since he is no longer in the hospital

followUp.rationale: The peak value describes what happened two weeks ago. It is not a baseline and is not a comparator; a single point-of-care value today would need serial sampling to mean anything, and nothing about it should delay transport.
